wcreq_kealey_1981.title: Gregory S. Kealey, “Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s,” Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981): 67–94.
wcreq_kealey_1981.citation: Gregory S. Kealey, “Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s,” Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981): 67–94.

verification.note: Abstract read: a contribution to the debate on the direction of social and working-class history, commenting on periodization, regionalism, ethnicity and culture; class analysis and the utility of culture for the study of Canadian workers are strongly defended. End page inferred from Bercuson’s start page; confirm. Checked against: Crossref DOI record; OpenAlex abstract (English and French). Addendum 2026-10-13: Pages 67–68 and 82–87 read closely with their footnotes; the rest skimmed by keyword (Érudit PDF, id.erudit.org/iderudit/llt7cri01; Critiques section, pp. 67–94, which also confirms the end page the existing record inferred). p. 67: the moment for evaluating the labour history of the 1960s–70s has arrived, signalled in Britain by the confrontation of “Althusserian structuralism and Thompsonian ‘culturalist’ or ‘socialist-humanist’ history”. p. 68: names McNaught’s forthcoming “E.P. Thompson vs. Harold Logan” as making “only too clear the eminently political nature of the emerging debate”. pp. 82–83: The Making of the English Working Class “has probably been the most influential piece of historical writing in the English language published since 1960”; “For our purposes, Thompson’s influence is our concern”; in North America “the critics are most often anti-Marxists attacking works which have associated themselves with Thompson’s method”. p. 87: quotes Bercuson (1979) accusing working-class historians of paying “due obeisance to E.P. Thompson, the guru” and “shoehorning their subjects into a Thompsonian mould”, and concedes that those “who utilize the insights of British … social history” must “demonstrate convincingly that they apply to the Canadian context”. The footnotes to these pages were read; the rest of the essay was skimmed by keyword only. Addendum 2026-10-14: Read in full for the 1.138 Kealey draft in the journal's PDF (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/2657; OJS metadata confirms pp. 67–94 and gives Memorial University). Not a reply to Bercuson's essay: p. 68 calls it 'This essay and the following contribution by David Bercuson', and its starred note says 'Both essays were delivered at the McGill Conference, "Class and Culture: Dimensions of Canada's Labour Past," 7-8 March 1980', revised 'extensively'. It answers Bercuson's 1979 charge of 'obeisance to E.P. Thompson, the guru' (p. 87). Further passages: the project 'always placed the relationship between classes at the centre of the story' (p. 69); the four-stage periodization (p. 74); region 'increasingly misplaced' as 'the crucial variable', 'western exceptionalism', n. 25 'David Bercuson has been most guilty of this', 'everything was different everywhere' (pp. 74–77); ethnicity and 'the official ethnic interpreters' (pp. 77–80); Gutman's influence on Palmer's and Kealey's books (p. 82 n. 33); 'the materiality of culture itself' (p. 85); 'Class-for-itself' (p. 86); 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history' (p. 89); McKay's unpublished paper 'one of the most substantive critiques of Thompson and culturalism' (p. 91 n.); the 1970s cohort 'active in the new left and influenced by the rebirth of Marxist scholarship' (p. 93).

wcreq_kealey_1981.scope_note: Kealey’s defence of class analysis and culture in the 1981 exchange.
